extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, logicians, and students concerned with definitions and scientific terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to form, evaluate, and revise precise connotations/definitions for terms in science and philosophy, including when to restrict or extend meanings and how definitions relate to discovery and propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with received use
rubrics_metrics.description: The fixed and precise connotation which [a term] receives should not be in deviation from, but in agreement (as far as it goes) with, the vague and fluctuating connotation which the term already had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fixing the connotation of a name that is already in use, define it so that it still denotes the things commonly denoted and does not render received assertions inadmissible; prefer definitions consistent with existing usage unless there is a deliberate and justified reason to depart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select properties that best mark the class
rubrics_metrics.description: To fix the connotation of a name we must select from among the various attributes in which the denoted objects agree; prefer properties on which many others depend, or which are sure marks from which many others will follow by inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit choice by preference for well-known properties but prioritize those that are explanatory or diagnostic (causal/dependent) so the definition enables inference to other properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must serve propositions / be useful
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition has scientific value only when we have under our consideration some proposition in which the term is employed; the question really is, how the conception shall be understood and defined in order that the proposition may be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what principle or proposition the proposed definition is meant to express; avoid arbitrary definitions unconnected to the use to which the term will be put.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as part of discovery — define after knowing the truth to state
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of definition is part of the business of discovery ... When it has been clearly seen what ought to be our definition, it must be pretty well known what truth we have to state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect to frame perfect definitions until sufficient knowledge/theory exists; definition often follows a decided step in knowledge and presupposes understanding of relevant facts and relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve essential established propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The settlement of a definition often involves the determination of propositions already assumed (e.g., in the debate about momentum, the proposition that momentum lost by one is equal to that gained by another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a definition, consider which established propositions it must preserve; definitions may be chosen so as to retain important experimentally or theoretically supported truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-obvious but diagnostic properties when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often necessary to define the class by some property not familiarly known, provided that property be the best mark of those which are known (example: defining life by continual decomposition-recomposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insist on only obvious predicates; prefer the property that best identifies the class even if it is less familiar to unscientific observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restriction to unwarranted extension
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better, in such a case, to give a fixed connotation to the term by restricting, than by extending its use; rather excluding from the epithet some things to which it is commonly considered applicable, than leaving out of its connotation any of the qualities previously pointed at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a term's common applications include heterogeneous items, restrict the definition to preserve the distinctive qualities that the term traditionally (even if vaguely) signalled, rather than extending the term to cover all merely similar or agreeable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain historical connotations; know the word's history before redefining
rubrics_metrics.description: In attempting to rectify the use of a vague term by giving it a fixed connotation, we must take care not to discard (unless advisedly) any portion of the connotation which the word previously carried; whoever seeks to introduce a more correct use should possess an accurate acquaintance with the history of the particular word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat language as a conservator of experience: investigate prior meanings and the propositions that depended on them before altering a term's connotation, because losing parts of meaning can lose past truths and insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain predicates and propositions to keep meanings alive
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of predicating of the name all the various properties which it originally connoted keeps up the association; propositions cannot keep the meaning of words alive if the meaning of the propositions themselves should die.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conscious predication and keep propositions meaningful rather than mechanically repeating formulas; ensure predicates themselves retain association with the intended properties so meanings do not fade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anchoring definitions to the weakest current usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons seeking definite language may examine old formulas and define the name without reference to the lost parts of its meaning, thus fastening down the name to what it connotes in common use at the time when it conveys the smallest quantity of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not fix a technical definition based only on the narrowest, most degraded current usage; beware that doing so may extend denotation beyond what was proper and discard valuable past meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and respect genuine ambiguity / multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: There are cases in which a word is used in two or more senses derived from each other, but yet radically distinct ... where the association is so slight and casual the several meanings will remain distinct; and where there is no one common property, defining so that one term covers all is often futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when a term's different senses have no shared essential property and avoid forcing one unified definition; accept multiple senses or use distinct terms to avoid false generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the history of a word as guide rather than just the dictionary
rubrics_metrics.description: The history of a word, by showing the causes which determine its use, is in many cases a better guide to its employment than any definition; definitions can only show its meaning at a particular time, but history may show the law by which the succession was produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult etymology, previous usages, and the chain of associative transitions ('transitive applications') to understand subtle shades and to inform responsible redefinition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that casual associations become part of connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any circumstance casually found along with a name may become associated with it so strongly that people give up using the name when that circumstance does not exist; the circumstance originally casual thus becomes regularly a part of the connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or prescribing usage, look for frequently co-occurring accidental features that may have become implicit in current sense; explicitly decide whether such accretions should be retained or discarded.
